extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent practitioners drafting patent specifications (patent attorneys, draughtsmen, inventors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing a patent specification: what must be disclosed, how to describe machines, substances, combinations and improvements, and what omissions or over-claims render a specification invalid. Focuses on disclosure duties and form of description so the public can practise the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and fair disclosure of all known matters
rubrics_metrics.description: To support a patent, it is necessary that the specification should make a full and fair disclosure to the public of all that is known to the patentee respecting his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it does not, the consideration on which he obtains his patent fails. Examples: representing several things as competent to produce a specific effect when only one will answer; suppressing anything which he knows will answer. Case law cited where patents were void for insufficient disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of the best and most improved state known
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject be not given to the public in the best and most improved state known to the inventor, the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor was acquainted with a mode of making the manufacture more beneficial than the one specified and conceals it, that concealment is fraudulent (e.g., steel trusses tempered with tallow; verdigris made with aqua fortis omitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Must disclose advantageous alterations or improvements known before grant
rubrics_metrics.description: No alteration, known to the inventor before he procures the patent, may be omitted, however insignificant, without raising a presumption of fraudulent concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small improvements (e.g., bending teeth of a lace machine or making one tooth longer) must be disclosed if known at grant time; omission may render patent void even if inadvertent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose improvements known before specification/enrolment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of a person taking out a patent to communicate to the public any improvement that he may make upon his invention before the specification has been enrolled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improvements are discovered in the period between grant and enrolment, they must be disclosed in the specification; the patentee may have time to bring invention to perfection but must still communicate intermediate improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent discoveries after grant do not vitiate the grant
rubrics_metrics.description: If a better mode of using the manufacture is a subsequent discovery after the date of the grant, the grant will continue valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There remains, however, a presumption of concealment against the patentee which may be rebutted by evidence that the improvement was made after grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must not be more extensive than the invention (no over-claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant must not be more extensive than the invention; the specification will be incorrect if it contains a description of more than the improvement or addition, unless it particularly distinguishes the new from the old parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee cannot monopolize the whole subject when his patent is only for an improvement. Examples include chairs and lever cases where a specification that encompassed prior art rendered the patent invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and sufficiency for a person of reasonable skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of a machine must be minute without perplexity, and luminous without being overwrought; it should be such that a common mechanic, with a reasonable degree of skill upon the subject, may comprehend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It need not teach a person ignorant of first principles, nor require the reader to exercise inventive faculty. A reasonable knowledge and skill (for which the jury decides) must be possessed by the person complaining that the specification is obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need for inventive faculty nor undue experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: No contrivance or addition, no trial or experiment, must be resorted to for a full knowledge of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is limited: trials that are not essentially necessary may be made. If the inventor leaves anything to be found out by experiment, the specification is bad unless the data, manner of performing, and expected results are so clearly given that it may easily be done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit references to external scientific works
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference may be made to the rudiments of the science by which the principles of the machine are explained, but not to scientific books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposition or truth generally known needs no reference; that which can be found only in a particular treatise must be explained within the specification and not merely referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed disclosure of machinery parts and relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: If contemplating a piece of machinery, the several parts (wheels, rollers, screws, springs, etc.) must be set forth, together with the proportion of their diameters, thickness, tension, etc., and the method by which they are united and the relative velocities of the movable parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts are removable during operation or different articles are intended to be worked upon, the specification must state which parts, their proportions for different purposes, and where they are to be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularize new parts and distinguish old parts in improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patent is for an improvement, the inventor may either describe the whole machine and particularize the addition, or describe the whole and point out which parts are old; but the new parts must be accurately distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are several acceptable ways to draft an improvement's specification: (1) describe whole and particularize the addition; (2) describe whole and point out old/not material parts; (3) describe the improvement and how applied to old parts; (4) describe whole and refer to former patent. The choice depends on intelligibility and avoiding over-claiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming combinations of known parts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a combination of substances, materials, or machine parts in common use previously applied for same or different purposes is claimed, the specification may set out the whole as the invention provided it clearly expresses that it is the new combination only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing more than the invention must be claimed. Every old part which is essential and material in producing the intended effect will be considered as claimed if not designated as old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe only the new combinations when adding to existing combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention consists of a new set of combinations added to a manufacture composed of combinations, the specification should only describe the new combinations which have been invented and how they are to be added to the old ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming antecedent combinations not invented by the patentee; if a prior combination existed up to a given point and the inventor's contribution is only subsequent combinations, the specification must not claim the whole earlier combination as his invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior/expired patents in combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the combination consists of the subjects of several expired patents (or bought ones), a description of the method by which they were combined, with a reference to the several specifications, will be sufficient to sustain the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciting and referring to enrolled prior patents is acceptable because they are matter of public record; careful explanation of the method of combination is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/principle claims require the same rigour as tangible means
rubrics_metrics.description: If a method is the subject of a patent (in practice the tangible means carrying the method into effect), the description must be very accurate and so clear and evident that no experiments are necessary to learn and put it in practice as beneficially as the patentee enjoys it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications of methods are governed by the same rules as machines, improvements, or combinations — precise, enabling disclosure without need for inventive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical inventions: disclose ingredients and process details
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chemical discovery is the foundation of the invention, the substance (not the principle) should be described: the ingredients, their proportions, the time of mixing, etc., ought to be fully stated and the beneficial uses explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must enable making the substance in the same way and with the same advantages as the inventor; concealment of a valuable additive (e.g., aqua fortis) destroyed patents in cases cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign manufactures must be fully and correctly explained
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacture first introduced into England (whether substance or machine, improvement, or combination) must be fully and correctly explained; its specification is regulated by the same laws as an English invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat foreign-origin inventions as requiring scrupulous disclosure of new parts and best modes; do not assume leniency because of origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every new part, however minute, must be clearly described
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part which is new, however minute, must be clearly described. In the specification of a substance, the simplest elements and the best modes of making and using it must be accurately stated; in machines, provide scrupulous fidelity about cheapest materials and exact proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public must be enabled at patent expiration to make the invention with the same advantages; concealment of any advantage or cheaper materials used in practice undermines the specification (patent may be void).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim multiple competent means if only one works
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee represents several things as competent to produce a specific effect when only one will answer, that is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to assert several equivalent means as workable if only one is operative; such misrepresentation can invalidate the patent.
